lesson.title: How Close Is Close Enough: Bond Length and Bond Order
lesson.summary: Bond length, the average distance between two bonded nuclei, shrinks as bond order rises, giving chemists a direct, measurable link between a Lewis structure and the real geometry of a molecule.
lesson.body:
Bond length is the average distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, measured at the point where attractive and repulsive forces between them balance out. It might seem like an atom's size alone should determine this distance, and atomic size does matter a great deal, but for a given pair of elements, bond order is the dominant factor: more shared electron pairs pull the two nuclei closer together, so bond length drops sharply as bond order rises.

Carbon-carbon bonds show this trend cleanly because so many real molecules contain all three bond orders. A typical C-C single bond, as in ethane, measures about 154 picometers. A C=C double bond, as in ethylene, measures about 134 picometers, noticeably shorter. A C-C triple bond, as in acetylene, the molecule from the triple bonds section, measures about 120 picometers, shorter still. Going from bond order 1 to 2 to 3 steadily pulls the two carbon nuclei closer together as more shared electron density accumulates between them.

Nitrogen shows the identical pattern with even more dramatic numbers, since nitrogen's triple bond is unusually strong. A typical N-N single bond runs about 145 picometers, an N=N double bond about 125 picometers, and the N-N triple bond in nitrogen gas about 110 picometers, among the shortest common bonds in chemistry. Chemists measure these distances experimentally using techniques such as X-ray crystallography and microwave or infrared spectroscopy, which is how the picometer level precision behind every value in this section was originally determined. Comparing these values against the carbon series shows that both bond order and the identity of the bonded atoms matter: nitrogen atoms are smaller than carbon atoms, so nitrogen's bonds at every bond order run shorter than carbon's equivalent bond order.

Fractional bond orders from resonance produce fractional, in between bond lengths, exactly as you would predict. Ozone's O-O bonds, at a bond order of 1.5, measure about 128 picometers, between a typical O-O single bond, about 148 pm, and an O=O double bond, about 121 pm. Benzene's carbon-carbon bonds, also at a bond order of 1.5, measure about 139 picometers, between the 154 pm single bond and 134 pm double bond you just saw in the carbon series. In both cases, the measured bond length lines up with the averaged bond order almost exactly as the resonance hybrid model predicts.

This bond order to bond length relationship is one of the clearest places where Lewis structure theory meets real, measurable chemistry: you can predict, just from counting shared electron pairs on paper, which bonds in a molecule will be shorter and stronger and which will be longer and weaker, and then confirm that prediction against experimentally measured distances. It is also a preview of bond energy, since shorter bonds generally require more energy to break, tying structure, distance, and reactivity together into one consistent picture.
